title: Memory, I/O interfacing and interrupts
subtitle: Connecting real chips to the bus so the processor reaches each one at exactly the right address.

sections.title: Address decoding
sections.body: Each memory or I/O chip has a chip-select input; address decoding turns the high address lines into select signals so exactly one chip responds. Full (unique) decoding uses all the high lines, so each location has one address; partial (non-unique) decoding ignores some, so the chip appears at several addresses (simpler hardware). Decoders (74LS138 3-to-8) or NAND gates generate the selects.

worked.why: An 8 KB RAM (2000H–3FFFH) on an 8085. Which lines select it?
8 KB = 2¹³, so A0–A12 go to the chip. The range 2000H–3FFFH has A15A14A13 = 001.

questions.prompt: Why must address decoding ensure only one chip responds?

choices.text: Two chips driving the data bus at once would cause bus contention and corrupt data.

figures.caption: Figure 4.1.1 — a decoder selects a chip
figures.note: Three upper address lines pick one 8 KB block.
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
[A15 A14 A13] as hi #blue
[3-to-8 decoder] as dec #violet
[Y0 → ROM 0000-1FFF] as y0 #mint
[Y1 → RAM 2000-3FFF] as y1 #mint
[Y2 → PPI 4000-5FFF] as y2 #amber
hi -> dec
dec -> y0 : 000
dec -> y1 : 001
dec -> y2 : 010");

problems.prompt: A 4 KB ROM must start at 4000H. What is its address range, and which address lines are decoded?
problems.answer: 4 KB = 2¹² → 12 lines on the chip (A0–A11). Range 4000H–4FFFH; A15–A12 = 0100 must be decoded.

sections.title: Memory-mapped I/O versus I/O-mapped I/O
sections.body: In memory-mapped I/O a device lives in the memory address space, so ordinary instructions (MOV, LDA, STA) access it, at the cost of memory addresses. In I/O-mapped (isolated) I/O a separate 256-port space is reached by IN and OUT with the IO/M̅ line high; the memory map stays free.

questions.prompt: Which instructions access an I/O-mapped device on the 8085?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: They assert IO/M̅ so memory does not respond.

sections.title: Parallel interface: the 8255 PPI
sections.body: The 8255 gives three 8-bit ports (A, B, C) programmed through a control word. Mode 0: simple input/output; Mode 1: strobed I/O with handshake; Mode 2: bidirectional. Handshaking: the device signals “data ready”, the processor reads and acknowledges — needed when the two run at different speeds.

worked.why: Program the 8255: port A output, port B input, port C output, Mode 0. Control word: D7 = 1 (mode set), D6–D5 = 00, D4 = 0 (A out), D3 = 0 (C upper out), D2 = 0, D1 = 1 (B in), D0 = 0 (C lower out).

choices.text: So fast and slow devices transfer data without loss.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each side waits for the other’s signal.

sections.title: Serial interface
sections.body: Serial transmission sends bits one after another. Asynchronous: each character is framed by a start bit (0) and stop bit(s) (1) so the receiver re-synchronises every byte; synchronous: a continuous block with a shared clock or sync characters, more efficient. RS-232 defines voltage levels and a 9/25-pin connector; USB is the modern serial bus; the 8251 USART does the conversion. Baud 9600 with 8N1 frames (10 bits/char) moves 960 characters/s.

worked.why: A link at 9600 baud sends 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit (8N1).
Bits per character = 1 start + 8 data + 1 stop = 10, so characters per second = 9600/10.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the start bit in asynchronous serial?

choices.text: It marks the beginning of a character so the receiver can synchronise its clock.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The line idles high; the falling edge is the signal.

sections.title: Interrupts
sections.body: Polling asks the device repeatedly; an interrupt lets the device ask for attention, so the CPU does useful work meanwhile. The 8085 has five hardware interrupts in priority order: TRAP (non-maskable), RST7.5, RST6.5, RST5.5 and INTR; each RST has a fixed vector (RST7.5 → 003CH, 6.5 → 0034H, 5.5 → 002CH, TRAP → 0024H). EI/DI enable and disable maskable interrupts; SIM/RIM set and read the masks. Processing: finish the instruction, push PC, jump to the vector, run the service routine, RET/EI.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It is non-maskable and highest priority.

figures.caption: Figure 5.1.1 — 8085 interrupt processing
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[Main program] as p
[8085] as c
[ISR at vector] as i
p -> c : executing
c -> c : interrupt request, EI is on
c -> i : push PC, jump to vector
i -> i : service the device
i --> c : EI, RET
c --> p : resume at the pushed PC");

sections.title: 8086 interrupts and the vector table
sections.body: The 8086 supports 256 interrupt types. Type n has a 4-byte entry (IP then CS) at address 4n in the interrupt vector table occupying 0000H–03FFH. Sources: hardware (NMI type 2, INTR with type from the PIC), software (INT n) and exceptions (divide error type 0, single-step type 1, breakpoint type 3, overflow type 4). The 8259 PIC prioritises up to 8 (cascaded, 64) devices.

worked.why: Where is the vector for interrupt type 21H?
Address = 4 × 21H = 84H; the four bytes at 0084H–0087H hold IP then CS of the handler.

sections.title: Advanced topics: RISC, CISC, control, DSP
sections.body: Accumulator-based machines (8085) route every result through A; register-based machines (8086 and later) use many registers. Hardwired control is fast; microprogrammed control is flexible. RISC (few simple instructions, pipelined) versus CISC (many complex ones). Multitasking needs protection and memory management support; a digital signal processor adds hardware multiply–accumulate and Harvard buses for real-time filtering.

questions.prompt: What operation do DSPs optimise above all?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Filters and transforms are sums of products.

problems.prompt: Give one reason a DSP uses a Harvard architecture.
problems.answer: It can fetch an instruction and two data operands in the same cycle, sustaining one multiply–accumulate per cycle for filters.
